title: The difference of two affine basic sets is a finite disjoint union of affine basic sets
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and write $D(f)=\{\mathfrak p:f\notin\mathfrak p\}$ and $V(g_1,\dots,g_n)=\{\mathfrak p:g_1,\dots,g_n\in\mathfrak p\}$ in $\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. If $B=D(f)\cap V(g_1,\dots,g_r)$ and $C=D(h)\cap V(k_1,\dots,k_s)$ are basic subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}A$, then $B\setminus C$ is a finite pairwise-disjoint union of basic subsets (the empty union is allowed).

source.place: Etale Cohomology, Lemma Tag 03S0, proof at line 12049 (the refinement is asserted there); the finite set calculation below is written out from the basic-set description of Algebra, Lemma Tag 0G1P

proof.text:
Conventions. Points of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ are the prime ideals $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], $D(a)=\{\mathfrak p: a
otin\mathfrak p\}$ and $V(a_1,\dots,a_n)=\{\mathfrak p: a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathfrak p\}$ (for $n=0$, $V()=\operatorname{Spec}A$). Two facts used below: (i) $V(a_1,\dots,a_n)\cap V(b_1,\dots,b_m)=V(a_1,\dots,a_n,b_1,\dots,b_m)$, directly from the definition; (ii) $D(a)\cap D(b)=D(ab)$: if $a
otin\mathfrak p$ and $b
otin\mathfrak p$ then $ab
otin\mathfrak p$ because $\mathfrak p$ is prime, and if $ab
otin\mathfrak p$ then $a
otin\mathfrak p$ and $b
otin\mathfrak p$ because $\mathfrak p$ is an ideal. Hence a finite intersection of sets $D(a)$ and $V(\dots)$ containing at least one $D(\cdot)$ is basic: $D(a_1)\cap\dots\cap D(a_p)\cap V(b_1,\dots,b_q)=D(a_1\cdots a_p)\cap V(b_1,\dots,b_q)$.

proof.text: The pieces. Put $P_0=B\cap V(h)=D(f)\cap V(g_1,\dots,g_r,h)$ and, for $j=1,\dots,s$, $P_j=B\cap D(h)\cap V(k_1,\dots,k_{j-1})\cap D(k_j)=D(fhk_j)\cap V(g_1,\dots,g_r,k_1,\dots,k_{j-1})$; the equalities hold by (i) and (ii) of the first step, so all $s+1$ pieces are basic. Case (a) of the second step says exactly $\mathfrak p\in P_0$, and case (b) with least index $j$ says exactly $\mathfrak p\in P_j$. Inclusion $B\setminus C\subseteq P_0\cup\dots\cup P_s$: a point of $B\setminus C$ is in case (a) or (b), hence in $P_0$ or in $P_j$ for its least index $j$. Inclusion $P_0\cup\dots\cup P_s\subseteq B\setminus C$: every $P_j$ lies in $B$; a point of $P_0$ has $h\in\mathfrak p$, so it is not in $D(h)\supseteq C$; a point of $P_j$ ($j\ge1$) has $k_j\notin\mathfrak p$, so it is not in $V(k_1,\dots,k_s)\supseteq C$. Hence $B\setminus C=P_0\cup P_1\cup\dots\cup P_s$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0G1P (label lemma-constructible, line 5434): the basic sets D(f) ∩ V(g_1,…,g_m); the set calculation is written out by the agent for the refinement asserted in Etale Cohomology, Lemma Tag 03S0 (etale-cohomology.tex, proof at line 12049)

proof.text: Pairwise disjointness. $P_0\cap P_j=\emptyset$ for $j\ge1$: points of $P_0$ have $h\in\mathfrak p$, points of $P_j$ have $h\notin\mathfrak p$. For $1\le j<j'\le s$, $P_j\cap P_{j'}=\emptyset$: points of $P_j$ have $k_j\notin\mathfrak p$, while points of $P_{j'}$ lie in $V(k_1,\dots,k_{j'-1})$ and so have $k_j\in\mathfrak p$. Therefore $B\setminus C$ is the pairwise-disjoint union of the $s+1$ basic sets $P_0,\dots,P_s$ (some of which may be empty; a family with empty members is still a finite pairwise-disjoint family of basic sets, and empty members may also be dropped).
